## A03 Jewish Unschooling: Autonomy With Structure

Route: `/blog/jewish-unschooling-torah`  
Topic: Motivation and Agency  
Search title: Jewish Unschooling and Torah Self-Governance | Bnei Neviim  
Search description: Autonomy, agency, and shared responsibility in a Torah learning community, with guidance, personal commitments, and room to rebuild motivation.

Jewish unschooling does not mean doing nothing. It does not mean hefker. It does not mean a boy runs the room, ignores adults, and calls that autonomy.

Jewish unschooling means that we take the inner world of the child seriously. Many boys have been trained to move only when someone pushes them: a prize, a threat, a grade, a punishment, a test, a speech, or a disappointed adult.

After years of that, a boy can lose touch with his own desire to learn. He may not know what he wants, what he is good at, what kind of person he wants to become, or what it feels like to choose something because it is true.

Some boys need a period of decompression. Decompression is not laziness. Here, it means time to unwind pressure and rebuild the ability to think independently.

But in a Torah environment, decompression must happen with structure. A boy is not told to do whatever he wants. He is asked what he thinks, what his options are, what will happen if he chooses this, and whether this choice fits the person he wants to become.

Bnei Neviim uses personal goals, honest conversations, movement, and Torah discussion to help boys rebuild ownership. The adult does not disappear. The adult becomes a mentor who helps the boy think and choose.

The point is not to replace one external control system with another. The point is to help the boy develop [self-governance](#a09-self-governance-in-jewish-education), so Torah becomes connected to his real choices and not only to compliance.

Bnei Neviim's morning Torah learning pods combine autonomy, agency, and shared responsibility.

A boy can be bribed into sitting. He can be threatened into opening a book. He can be pressured into repeating the right words. But none of that means he has begun to love Torah.

Prizes and pressure may create short-term compliance. They may make the adult feel that something is happening. But if a boy learns only because someone is pushing him, the learning is still outside of him.

Difficulties are addressed through [private coaching](#a06-why-boys-need-private-mentorship-not-just-classes) and follow-up. The correction is meant to build awareness, not shame.

The goal is not to make Torah easy. The goal is to make Torah real. Real Torah learning asks a boy to think, listen, choose, and connect the ideas to his own life.

If your son needs Torah learning that builds inner responsibility instead of fake motivation, speak with Bnei Neviim.

## A06 Why Boys Need Private Mentorship, Not Just Classes

Route: `/blog/private-mentorship-for-boys`  
Topic: Responsibility and Self-Governance  
Search title: Private Rebbe Mentorship for Boys | Bnei Neviim  
Search description: Private mentorship helps boys clarify goals, take responsibility, and connect Torah to real decisions.

Classes matter. A good class can teach Chumash, halacha, hashkafa, and skills. But many boys need more than a class. They need a relationship in which their real questions, choices, and patterns can be spoken about honestly.

## A08 The Parent's Role in an Alternative Torah Learning Program

Route: `/blog/parents-role-autonomous-learning`  
Topic: Parents and Community  
Search title: Parent Partnership in Alternative Torah Learning | Bnei Neviim  
Search description: Parents support autonomous Torah learning by coaching instead of controlling and helping their son take real responsibility.

An alternative Torah learning program is not a place where parents outsource responsibility and wait for someone else to fix their son.

Parents are partners. That does not mean parents need to hover, manage every detail, or turn every conversation into a lecture. It means the language at home needs to support the same goal: ownership.

A boy who is learning [self-governance](#a09-self-governance-in-jewish-education) needs adults around him who ask better questions. What did you commit to? What happened? What did you learn about yourself? What is your next honest step?

If the home message is only prizes, threats, and power struggles, the boy learns to negotiate with external pressure. If the home message is honest responsibility, the boy can begin to notice himself and choose more maturely.

Parents also need patience. Some boys who leave pressure-based schooling may need time to decompress and reconnect with learning. That process cannot be forced, but it also cannot be abandoned.

Bnei Neviim works best when parents support the same calm, direct language: dignity, responsibility, movement when needed, honest accountability, and connection to Torah as real life. Parents help their children arrive prepared, collaborate on goals, and share observations that inform coaching and follow-up.

Speak with Bnei Neviim about how parent partnership supports your son's growth.

## A09 Self-Governance in Jewish Education

Route: `/blog/self-governance-in-jewish-education`  
Topic: Responsibility and Self-Governance  
Search title: Self-Governance in Jewish Education | Raising Responsible Torah Boys  
Search description: Self-governance connects actions with Torah values through agency, agreed commitments, meaningful responsibility, and reflection.

Self-governance is not the same as independence without guidance. It means a boy is learning to govern himself according to Torah, reality, and responsibility.

Many school systems train children to wait for external control. Sit because the adult said so. Learn because there is a test. Behave because there is a punishment. Perform because there is a reward.

Those tools may produce order, but they do not necessarily produce a boy who can make good choices when no one is watching.

At Bnei Neviim, commitments are agreed in relation to each boy's level. [Private review](#a06-why-boys-need-private-mentorship-not-just-classes) considers what was completed, its difficulty, what helped, and what got in the way. Responsibility also takes form in work the community needs: caring for shared spaces and following through on agreed roles.

Self-governance includes consequences, but not humiliation. It includes autonomy, but not chaos. It includes adult leadership, but not constant control.

The aim is for a boy to connect his actions to his values. What kind of Jew do I want to be? What does Hashem want from me right now? What did I choose today, and what will I choose tomorrow?

Learn more about how Bnei Neviim builds self-governance through Torah learning, mentorship, and accountability.

## A11 A Guide to Healthy Technology Use: Our Philosophy and Approach

Route: `/blog/healthy-technology-use-jewish-children`  
Topic: Technology  
Search title: Healthy Technology Use for Jewish Children | Bnei Neviim  
Search description: A Torah-based approach to technology: abstinence, limited use, holistic use, and practical boundaries for children.

There are three basic philosophies to the approach of technology usage.

### The Abstinence Approach

The Abstinence Approach views technology as a significant distraction from spiritual growth. It advocates avoiding technology in order to focus on serving Hashem. This was my experience during my years in yeshiva, where I completely disconnected from technology, allowing me to fully immerse myself in Torah study.

**Pros:** The benefits of this approach can be profound, particularly for those who seek to excel in learning Gemara within a yeshiva setting. Engaging fully in Torah study without the distractions of technology allows time for concentration and spiritual connection. I found that commitment valuable in learning how to learn.

**Cons:** There are significant downsides to this approach. Professional life often involves tools such as messaging and email. Avoiding these tools can restrict the work a person is able to do and the educational material he can access. There is also a social question: how do we explain our boundaries to children without belittling people who live differently? A boundary that adults have chosen with conviction may be harder for their children to understand.

I personally know individuals who have chosen this path despite its challenges. They have made this decision with full awareness of the difficulties, guided by their Rabbis and driven by their commitment to what they believe is the best way to raise their children in a world where no ideology is foolproof. These individuals deserve great respect for the conviction behind their decision. I think of the verses שומר פתאים ה׳ and עדות ה׳ נאמנה מחכימת פתי, and the trust in Hashem expressed by that way of life.

### The Limited Use Approach

The Limited Use Approach advocates cautious engagement with technology, allowing its use for positive purposes while remaining vigilant against its dangers. In a conversation with Rabbi Daniel Travis, we discussed the distinction between broad warnings about internet use and a person's individual circumstances. During that conversation, he described internet use as a spiritual compromise that is often necessary for functioning in the modern world.

**Pros:** This approach provides access to online learning and tools for earning a livelihood. It was spectacular to witness during the COVID-19 pandemic when the lectures of renowned Rabbis reached students thousands of miles away through the internet.

**Cons:** The downside to this approach is that involvement with technology is experienced as a spiritual compromise. For some, this perspective helps maintain their commitment to spirituality without getting carried away. For others, it can leave a significant portion of their life feeling בדיעבד—less than ideal.

### The Holistic Approach

The Holistic Approach views technology as a powerful tool that Hashem created to enhance spiritual growth. This philosophy embraces technology as a means to access wisdom and disseminate positive messages. It incorporates the same safeguards as the previous approach but with a fundamental difference: the internet, technology, and physical engagement are seen as tools to be used for good, without inherently undermining a person's spiritual level. I connect this perspective with the emphasis in Chassidus on bringing avodas Hashem into physical life.

**Pros:** Wisdom that can aid in serving Hashem becomes something to seek out and put to use. Engaging with worthwhile material can be invigorating and can support a person's spiritual and practical goals.

**Cons:** Purposeful use still requires vigilance. A person can encounter inappropriate content or become involved in activities contrary to his values.

In practice, technology use should be tailored to an individual's stage of life and personal goals. If a person is in yeshiva and wants to immerse himself in learning, less technology may serve that goal. If someone needs the internet for work but struggles with its boundaries, the second approach may be appropriate.

Personally, I have adopted the third approach. I am constantly striving to maximize my life, even with the possibility of making mistakes. However, this is a decision that an adult can make. A child may not yet appreciate the consequences of the content he encounters or know how to manage it. The third approach requires honesty about failure, the ability to distinguish useful engagement from distraction, and the willingness to do Teshuvah and keep trying.

### For Children

For children, it is crucial to establish clear boundaries and introduce technology gradually, based on their maturity and responsibility levels. When my children asked for phones, I explained that when I see they are living responsible lives—abiding by their schedules, saying no to harmful behaviors, and staying motivated toward their goals—I will know they are ready to use a phone as a tool for enhancing their already structured and directed lives. Until then, it will not serve them well. They both understood this message clearly and agreed.

#### Educating Our Children About Technology

The most important aspect of educating our children about technology is honesty. This means explaining the internet and its risks openly, in a way appropriate to their age. The Torah that Hashem has given us can address the issues they face. Withholding information or pretending not to understand their questions makes it harder for them to turn to us.

We need our children to view us as relatable human beings, engaged in the struggles of life ourselves and concerned for their ultimate success. When such a relationship exists, they have someone to turn to when they encounter something confusing or inappropriate. I believe parents should begin these conversations before children are left to piece together an understanding from their peers.

### Movies, YouTube, and Video Games

#### Movies and YouTube

Media can carry ideas that conflict with Torah values even when it is not explicitly vulgar or violent. Innuendos, behavior, and the assumptions a story makes about a good life all deserve attention. When choosing something for a child to watch, look at the worldview it presents as well as its individual scenes.

#### Video Games

Video games are interactive, and some allow creativity. That alone is not a reason to treat them as beneficial or to allow unlimited use. The question is how a particular game fits into a child's life: can he stop at the agreed time, and does he still attend to his responsibilities?

Communication features matter too. Playing with others can expose a child to unfamiliar people and inappropriate language. Parents need to understand the actual game, its settings, and who their child is playing with.

#### Social Media

Social media requires particular caution. Comparison, public approval, and the pull to keep checking can become central to the experience. My approach is to keep children away from open-ended social media use. If an older child has a specific reason to use a platform, the purpose, boundaries, and adult involvement need to be clear.

#### Guidance on Media Choices

A valuable piece of advice I received from Rabbi Lippman was to review detailed descriptions of a movie's content before choosing it. Parents and children can then make an informed decision about themes such as sexual content, extreme violence, or disrespect toward others. The question is whether the particular content fits the values we are trying to live by.

### Practical Protocol

#### Create Playlists

Before letting your children watch YouTube, prepare a playlist. Choose the videos in advance so the session has a clear purpose and an endpoint. This also gives you a chance to review what they will watch.

#### Consider Peer Norms

Take into account the norms of your children's friends. A child may want to watch a show because it is part of the conversation around him. That social context deserves to be heard, even when you decide a particular show does not fit your family's boundaries.

I try to consider both the content and the child's relationship with his friends. Explain the decision honestly, and listen to what it means to him. Parents need to remain people their children can speak to about the life they are actually living.

#### Set Media Boundaries

Media consumption should be scheduled and purposeful. If a child always turns to a screen when he is bored, ask what else he wants to do with his time. In my approach, media is a privilege connected to demonstrated responsibility. It should fit into a life that already has direction.

#### Save Videos That Answer Real Questions

There is a lot of interesting content available. When children ask questions, remember to find relevant videos and save them to a playlist. That way, when they do watch something, it will address something that already interests them.

#### Keep Smartphones Out of Learning

Keep smartphones out of the learning session so the boys can attend to the learning and to one another. The current morning pods focus on Kodesh; this article describes the broader approach to technology and parenting.

Personally, I have adopted the third approach. I am constantly striving to maximize my life, even with the possibility of making mistakes. However, this is a decision that an adult can make. A child may not yet appreciate the consequences of the content he encounters or know how to manage it. The third approach requires honesty about failure, the ability to distinguish useful engagement from distraction, and the willingness to do Teshuvah and keep trying.

### For Children

For children, it is crucial to establish clear boundaries and introduce technology gradually, based on their maturity and responsibility levels. When my children asked for phones, I explained that when I see they are living responsible lives—abiding by their schedules, saying no to harmful behaviors, and staying motivated toward their goals—I will know they are ready to use a phone as a tool for enhancing their already structured and directed lives. Until then, it will not serve them well. They both understood this message clearly and agreed.

#### Educating Our Children About Technology

The most important aspect of educating our children about technology is honesty. This means explaining the internet and its risks openly, in a way appropriate to their age. The Torah that Hashem has given us can address the issues they face. Withholding information or pretending not to understand their questions makes it harder for them to turn to us.

We need our children to view us as relatable human beings, engaged in the struggles of life ourselves and concerned for their ultimate success. When such a relationship exists, they have someone to turn to when they encounter something confusing or inappropriate. I believe parents should begin these conversations before children are left to piece together an understanding from their peers.

### Movies, YouTube, and Video Games

#### Movies and YouTube

Media can carry ideas that conflict with Torah values even when it is not explicitly vulgar or violent. Innuendos, behavior, and the assumptions a story makes about a good life all deserve attention. When choosing something for a child to watch, look at the worldview it presents as well as its individual scenes.

#### Video Games

Video games are interactive, and some allow creativity. That alone is not a reason to treat them as beneficial or to allow unlimited use. The question is how a particular game fits into a child's life: can he stop at the agreed time, and does he still attend to his responsibilities?

Communication features matter too. Playing with others can expose a child to unfamiliar people and inappropriate language. Parents need to understand the actual game, its settings, and who their child is playing with.

#### Social Media

Social media requires particular caution. Comparison, public approval, and the pull to keep checking can become central to the experience. My approach is to keep children away from open-ended social media use. If an older child has a specific reason to use a platform, the purpose, boundaries, and adult involvement need to be clear.

#### Guidance on Media Choices

A valuable piece of advice I received from Rabbi Lippman was to review detailed descriptions of a movie's content before choosing it. Parents and children can then make an informed decision about themes such as sexual content, extreme violence, or disrespect toward others. The question is whether the particular content fits the values we are trying to live by.

### Practical Protocol

#### Create Playlists

Before letting your children watch YouTube, prepare a playlist. Choose the videos in advance so the session has a clear purpose and an endpoint. This also gives you a chance to review what they will watch.

#### Consider Peer Norms

Take into account the norms of your children's friends. A child may want to watch a show because it is part of the conversation around him. That social context deserves to be heard, even when you decide a particular show does not fit your family's boundaries.

I try to consider both the content and the child's relationship with his friends. Explain the decision honestly, and listen to what it means to him. Parents need to remain people their children can speak to about the life they are actually living.

#### Set Media Boundaries

Media consumption should be scheduled and purposeful. If a child always turns to a screen when he is bored, ask what else he wants to do with his time. In my approach, media is a privilege connected to demonstrated responsibility. It should fit into a life that already has direction.

#### Save Videos That Answer Real Questions

There is a lot of interesting content available. When children ask questions, remember to find relevant videos and save them to a playlist. That way, when they do watch something, it will address something that already interests them.

#### Keep Smartphones Out of Learning

Keep smartphones out of the learning session so the boys can attend to the learning and to one another. The current morning pods focus on Kodesh; this article describes the broader approach to technology and parenting.

## A14 Helping Boys Own Their Spirituality

Route: `/blog/kids-own-their-spirituality`  
Topic: Motivation and Agency  
Search title: Helping Boys Own Their Spirituality | Torah Self-Governance  
Search description: Boys need to learn how to ask what Hashem wants from them, not only copy someone else's spiritual path.

Children often begin by copying. That is natural. They copy parents, Rebbeim, friends, and community expectations.

But at some point, a boy needs to begin owning his avodas Hashem. He needs to ask what is true, what Hashem wants from him, what he is ready to accept, and where he needs to grow next.

Owning spirituality does not mean inventing your own Torah. It means [taking responsibility within Torah](#a09-self-governance-in-jewish-education). It means moving from external performance toward inner commitment.

Some boys resist religious life because it has felt like control. Others perform beautifully but do not yet know how to make independent spiritual choices.

Bnei Neviim helps boys practice responsibility in small daily ways: following through on an agreed learning commitment, noticing engagement, speaking honestly, and connecting Torah ideas to their own choices.

The long-term goal is a boy who is learning to ask what Hashem wants from him when he is the one making the decision.

Topic: Torah Learning  
Search title: How to Turn Spaced-Out Moments Into Torah Lessons | Bnei Neviim  
Search description: When boys drift from the text, a skilled Rebbe can meet them where they are and bring Torah into the conversation.

Every Rebbe knows the moment. The boy is in the room, but he is no longer with the learning. His eyes drift, his body moves, his mind goes somewhere else.

One response is to snap him back with shame. Another response is to ignore it. Neither one is usually enough.

A skilled Rebbe can sometimes meet the boy where he is and bring Torah into the conversation. What happened to your focus? Where did your mind go? What does that tell you about yourself? What would it mean to come back right now?

Every distraction does not need a long discussion. The adult is looking for the educational opportunity inside the moment.

A spaced-out moment can become a Torah lesson when it helps the boy understand his mind, his choices, and his responsibility.

## A18 Secular Studies: Torah, Livelihood, and Real Work

Route: `/blog/real-life-secular-learning-future-vision`  
Topic: Vision  
Search title: Torah, Livelihood, and Real-World Learning | Bnei Neviim  
Search description: The Academy 2027–28 vision for practical projects, entrepreneurship, financial literacy, and learning that connects responsibility with useful skills.

This article describes the [Academy 2027–28 vision](#p03-academy-202728). The current South Florida learning pods offer morning Kodesh. Practical projects and a full-day program belong to the Academy vision.

### A Father's Obligation to Teach His Son a Livelihood

Our Sages teach that a father is obligated to teach his son a trade (Kiddushin 29a). Chovot HaLevavot, Shaar HaBitachon, chapter 3, describes choosing an occupation suited to one's nature and abilities, accepting its demands, and trusting in Hashem. Livelihood can become a way to develop one's capabilities and put them to use in the world.

An education can leave a student with theoretical knowledge but little experience creating tangible value. The question we need to ask is how the skills a boy is learning will help him contribute, support himself, and take responsibility for his future family.

### Supervised Real Work Experience

In the Academy vision, students would be active contributors to meaningful work. Boys with an interest in business activities would have opportunities to learn entrepreneurship and financial literacy within a Torah-grounded environment. We believe that financial success is a tool for serving Hashem and living as a committed Jew. When a student expresses interest in building something of value, individualized guidance can help him identify personal goals, develop an idea, and refine the skills needed to bring it to life.

Responsibility has to match the individual boy's readiness. A student learning to use a tool may need close guidance. A boy who already knows how to perform a task may still need practice following through consistently. Gardening, irrigation, and drilling involve particular hard skills; independence, consistency, responsibility, and collaboration develop through repeated practice and follow-up.

### Two Forms of Practical Learning

The original vision brings together work that serves the learning community and projects that students initiate themselves.

#### Projects That Serve the Community

The Academy can become a place where boys help take care of the environment they use. Tutoring a younger student in a skill, organizing materials, maintaining a garden, or helping plan a trip gives a boy something useful to contribute. Each project needs a clear purpose, appropriate guidance, and a way to review the work.

Student budgeting, organization, decisions, and voting would take place within a defined scope. Boys need to understand what they are responsible for, what they can decide, and when an adult is responsible for the decision.

#### Independent Student Ventures

Students may also develop ideas of their own. An interest in a product, service, or small business can become a reason to learn numbers, writing, communication, planning, and the practical skills the idea requires. The educational aim is to help a boy carry an idea through into useful work, with realistic expectations and adult guidance.

### Why the Work Needs to Matter

When education feels like something being imposed on a student, he can lose sight of its value. A learning environment should help him take responsibility for what he is doing and why. The Academy vision combines student autonomy with agreed minimum commitments, so that individual direction and shared responsibility can work together.

An environment where students do real work for the benefit of the community gives them a reason to care about the outcome. With tools, materials, and coaching, they can produce something useful and see the consequences of their decisions. A garden needs tending after it has been planted. A trip plan has to fit the budget. Someone else may be relying on a task being finished.

Assignments that never connect to a purpose beyond the grade can leave students wondering why their effort matters. Practical work makes the purpose visible. It also creates a reason to return to the underlying skills: measuring accurately, writing clearly, checking a calculation, or explaining a decision.

The boys' contributions should be needed and valued. They are responsible for real tasks, given real tools, and taught how to use them. They can see the results of their contributions and experience being members of a functioning community.

### Free AI Software for Jewish Schools

The broader technology work brings the same concern for useful skills to schools and educators. Bnei Neviim offers [Free AI Software for Jewish Schools](#p10-technology): natural-language tools and custom automations intended to reduce administrative overhead.

A school can sign up and receive personal contact to discuss its needs. Understanding a real workflow, describing what needs to happen, and checking whether a tool does that job are all examples of purposeful work. These are also skills that can inform future educational projects.

The technology offer has its own page and support path. It is separate from the current morning Kodesh pods and from support for the wider Academy vision.

### Entrepreneurship and Jewish Identity

Rashi on Devarim 4:28 explains the verse's reference to serving other gods through subservience to the people who worship them. For me, this raises a broader question about livelihood: whose purposes are my time, energy, and talents advancing? That educational question is my application of the source.

Entrepreneurship gives a person an opportunity to build his own capabilities and take responsibility for the direction of his work. He has to think about the value he offers, the people he serves, and the commitments he makes. It can become an expression of his particular abilities within a life of avodas Hashem.

In our educational philosophy, secular skills are directed toward livelihood, practical responsibility, and serving Hashem. Understanding elements of the outside world can also deepen our understanding of Torah. The purpose of studying a skill should be clear to the student, and its use should remain connected to the life he is trying to build.

## A19 Ratzon and Intrinsic Motivation

Route: `/blog/ratzon-and-intrinsic-motivation`  
Topic: Motivation and Agency  
Search title: Ratzon and Intrinsic Motivation | Bnei Neviim Academy  
Search description: Ratzon, identity, and the desire to learn: BNA's approach to connecting Torah, personal meaning, agency, and sustained responsibility.

The same behavior can come from pressure or from ratzon. A boy may sit with a sefer because he expects a prize, because he is afraid to disappoint someone, or because the question in front of him matters to him. The outward action does not reveal the whole relationship to learning.

Ratzon means will or desire. In BNA's educational approach, the question is what a boy wants to move toward and how that direction connects to Torah, his values, and his understanding of who he is.

### Interest and identification

Enjoyment of learning itself and identification with the value of learning are related, but distinct. A boy may stay with a discussion because he finds it interesting. He may also persist through a difficult passage because understanding Torah matters to the person he wants to become.

Both belong in the educational picture. Intrinsic interest gives a reason to engage with the activity itself. Identification with a purpose gives the effort a place in his life. Ratzon should not be reduced to whether he enjoys every moment.

The aim is for Torah learning and serving Hashem to become part of his own direction. A completed page matters, and so does the relationship being formed with learning.

### Torah in response to a question

A question gives learning a purpose. A disagreement, a difficulty, or an observation can lead into Torah sources that address something the boys are already trying to understand.

This is the [organic flow of Torah](#a10-torah-that-answers-real-life): following the group's questions, identifying the relevant sources, and developing the discussion. The educator brings knowledge and direction while taking the boys' actual questions seriously.

Learning can then involve curiosity, effort, disagreement, and discovery. The boy has a question to work through and a reason to pursue an answer.

### Giving ratzon practical form

Agency requires opportunities to act and commitments to follow through. Coaching connects intention with action: what was agreed, what was completed, where difficulty arose, and what comes next. Goals are considered relative to each boy's level.

A difficult beginning does not mean there is no ratzon. It may call for a clearer purpose, an attainable next step, useful support, or a conversation about what the boy actually wants.

The educator also provides a [living example](#a22-role-models-or-pnimi-and-or-makif). Seeing someone take Torah, work, and other people seriously gives substance to the person a boy may want to become.

Ratzon gives direction to effort. The educational task is to help a boy recognize a direction he can own and develop the capacity to follow it.

## A20 Responsibility Through Meaningful Contribution

Route: `/blog/responsibility-through-meaningful-contribution`  
Topic: Responsibility and Self-Governance  
Search title: Responsibility Through Meaningful Contribution | Bnei Neviim Academy  
Search description: Responsibility develops through useful roles, clear commitments, practical contribution, and learning from the results of one's work.

Responsibility has to be practiced. Knowing what a responsible person should do is only a beginning. A boy needs a role, a purpose for that role, and an opportunity to experience what happens when he follows through or leaves the work unfinished.

BNA's approach begins with meaningful contribution. The student is needed. His work serves a real purpose within the institution, and he can see how his participation affects other people.

### A role with a purpose

A useful role makes the responsibility clear. There is something that needs to happen, someone who has agreed to take it on, and a standard by which the result can be assessed.

In the planned Academy 2027–28, this includes care of shared spaces, project organization, budgeting, trip planning, and participation in community decisions. Gardening and irrigation provide practical examples: plants need water, materials need to be organized, and a system needs to function.

The purpose of these tasks is visible. They contribute to the community's daily life. Skills are learned because the work requires them.

Agency matters here. Students participate in selecting and understanding their commitments. Once a role is accepted, its responsibilities become part of the agreement.

### Learning from the result

Real work provides feedback. An irrigation connection either supplies water where it is needed or requires adjustment. A budget either accounts for the planned expense or leaves something unresolved. A shared space is either ready for the next group or still needs attention.

The educator provides instruction, appropriate oversight, and support. The student needs room to attempt the work, make mistakes, and participate in correcting them.

Failure becomes part of the review: what happened, what was missed, what support was needed, and what needs to change. Completing the task for a boy before he can respond removes an opportunity to practice responsibility. Leaving him with a task he cannot understand removes the guidance he needs.

### Capability and follow-through

Technical ability and responsibility are assessed separately. A student may demonstrate how to use a tool correctly once. Consistent preparation, care of materials, appropriate collaboration, and independent follow-through require evidence across his work.

Review considers his level and the difficulty of the agreed task. It distinguishes what he can do from how reliably he applies that ability. A mistake informs the next step; it does not define the student.

[Self-governance](#a09-self-governance-in-jewish-education) develops within this relationship between agency and shared responsibility. The boy contributes to something he values, sees the effect of his choices, and has a part in improving the result.

## A21 Designing the Learning Environment

Route: `/blog/designing-the-learning-environment`  
Topic: Learning Environment  
Search title: Designing the Learning Environment | Bnei Neviim Academy  
Search description: The people, physical space, atmosphere, and resources around a boy are central to BNA's approach to Torah learning and self-governance.

The first educational decision is the environment a boy will spend his time in. Information is one part of that environment. The people around him, the way they relate to one another, the atmosphere they create, and the resources available all belong to the education.

BNA places the quality of this environment before the quantity of information delivered. The question is what kind of participation the setting invites and what kind of person it asks the boy to become.

### The people

The educator's life is part of the curriculum. How he listens, handles disagreement, responds to mistakes, and follows through on his own responsibilities gives the learning its daily context.

A lesson about respect has to exist in an atmosphere of respect. A discussion about responsibility has to take place among adults who accept responsibility. Interest in Torah has to be visible in the people teaching it.

This is why the [role model](#a22-role-models-or-pnimi-and-or-makif) matters. The boy encounters a person whose example gives substance to the ideas being discussed. Tone, patience, personal discipline, and the ability to remain engaged through difficulty are part of that example.

### The physical space

A learning space should support study, discussion, movement, and practical work. Its arrangement should make the activities understandable: where materials belong, what is needed for a task, and how the space is prepared for the next person.

The environment can carry some of the responsibility. Materials that have a clear place can be returned to that place. A shared work area can be prepared, used, and restored by those who depend on it.

Student participation in maintaining the space gives this order a purpose. The boys contribute to a place they use together.

### The resources

Resources should make it possible to pursue a question or complete useful work. A relevant sefer, an educator who can explain a difficult passage, suitable tools, and practical instruction each have a role.

Access alone is not the whole educational task. The student needs to learn how to identify what is needed, use it appropriately, evaluate the result, and seek help when necessary.

Technology belongs within this same purpose. It should support learning and useful work, with guidance appropriate to the task.

### A community that can learn

The atmosphere must allow honest questions, appropriate disagreement, and mistakes that can be examined and corrected. Shared responsibility gives students a reason to participate in decisions about the community.

These principles guide the planning of Academy 2027–28. The South Florida location is to be announced. The educational work begins with defining the people, relationships, responsibilities, and resources the setting must support.

[The BNA Vision](#p11-vision)

## A22 Role Models, Or Pnimi, and Or Makif

Route: `/blog/role-models-or-pnimi-or-makif`  
Topic: Learning Environment  
Search title: Role Models, Or Pnimi, and Or Makif | Bnei Neviim Academy  
Search description: BNA's educational use of Or Pnimi and Or Makif distinguishes instruction that becomes understood from inspiration through a living example.

An educator teaches information and skills, and also shows what a life built around Torah can look like. These are different aspects of chinuch, even when the same person provides both.

BNA uses the distinction between Or Pnimi and Or Makif to describe this relationship. This is an educational application of concepts from Chassidus: what has become understood and internalized, and what inspires a person beyond his present capacity.

### Or Pnimi: what can be internalized

Or Pnimi means internal light. In this educational application, it refers to teaching that enters the student's understanding: a word he can translate, a Rashi he can explain, a halacha he can apply, or a skill he can carry out.

Instruction has to meet the student's present level. A difficult passage may need to be divided into parts. An explanation may need an example. The educator observes what the boy can do independently and where support is still needed.

As understanding develops, the support can change. The aim is for the learning to become something the boy can use himself.

### Or Makif: what awakens aspiration

Or Makif means surrounding light. For BNA, it describes inspiration that reaches beyond what a student can yet explain or perform.

A boy may encounter someone whose seriousness in Torah, discipline in work, or conduct toward other people awakens a desire to grow. He may recognize a quality worth moving toward before he knows how to develop it.

Instruction can be broken into steps. The life being modeled remains whole. The educator can make a Rashi accessible without making his own commitment to Torah smaller. The boy can encounter that commitment and begin to imagine his own direction.

This is part of cultivating [ratzon](#a19-ratzon-and-intrinsic-motivation).

### The educator's example

Role modeling takes place in ordinary conduct: listening to an objection, acknowledging a mistake, caring for shared materials, keeping an agreement, and returning to a difficult question.

These moments show how the values being taught are lived. The example includes how the educator handles his own limitations and corrects his own work.

A role model does not remove the need for instruction. Inspiration needs opportunities for study, practice, and responsibility. Instruction also needs a purpose that makes the effort worth pursuing.

### Teaching at BNA

This distinction informs the educator's role at BNA: substantive Torah teaching, responsiveness to the group's questions, and individual coaching within an autonomous learning community.

When participation becomes difficult, the conversation returns to the student's commitment, the obstacle encountered, and the next practical step. Guidance should preserve dignity while taking responsibility seriously.

The educator brings both knowledge that can be understood and an example worth growing toward.

Instruction can be broken into steps. The life being modeled remains whole. The educator can make a Rashi accessible without making his own commitment to Torah smaller. The boy can encounter that commitment and begin to imagine his own direction.

This is part of cultivating [ratzon](#a19-ratzon-and-intrinsic-motivation).

### The educator's example

Role modeling takes place in ordinary conduct: listening to an objection, acknowledging a mistake, caring for shared materials, keeping an agreement, and returning to a difficult question.

These moments show how the values being taught are lived. The example includes how the educator handles his own limitations and corrects his own work.

A role model does not remove the need for instruction. Inspiration needs opportunities for study, practice, and responsibility. Instruction also needs a purpose that makes the effort worth pursuing.

### Teaching at BNA

This distinction informs the educator's role at BNA: substantive Torah teaching, responsiveness to the group's questions, and individual coaching within an autonomous learning community.

When participation becomes difficult, the conversation returns to the student's commitment, the obstacle encountered, and the next practical step. Guidance should preserve dignity while taking responsibility seriously.

The educator brings both knowledge that can be understood and an example worth growing toward.

## A23 Torah, Daas, and Inner Development

Route: `/blog/torah-daas-and-inner-development`  
Topic: Torah Learning  
Search title: Torah, Daas, and Inner Development | Bnei Neviim Academy  
Search description: BNA's Torah teaching philosophy: the relationship between spiritual influence, conscious understanding, personal questions, and Torah expressed in life.

### Two Forms of Divine Influence

Chassidus distinguishes between ממלא כל עלמין, Memaleh Kol Almin, and סובב כל עלמין, Sovev Kol Almin. Memaleh describes Divine influence received according to the capacity of each created being. Sovev describes influence that exceeds that capacity and is not consciously grasped in the same way. These are spiritual descriptions; encompassing does not mean occupying the space around an object.

The soul expresses different capacities through the eyes and the brain. This illustrates influence received according to the capacity of the recipient.

The distinction helps frame an educational question: what has a person already understood and internalized, and what is influencing or inspiring him beyond his present understanding? A person needs both. The encounter with something greater can awaken a desire to grow, while learning gives that growth a form he can understand and use.

### Mitzvos and Conscious Integration

A mitzvah has spiritual significance even when its meaning is not fully understood. At the same time, the work of avodas Hashem includes bringing more of that meaning into conscious life. A boy can learn what a mitzvah requires, consider what it expresses, and notice how it affects the way he relates to Hashem and other people.

The goal is integration: Torah knowledge becomes connected to awareness, judgment, and action. In this educational framework, daas concerns a relationship with what is known. Information has become personal enough to guide how a person lives.

This educational vision connects that process with Geulah and the coming of Moshiach: the revelation of Hashem’s oneness within the finite world. That purpose gives the work of bringing Torah and mitzvos into conscious life its wider direction.

### Torah as Guidance for the Person

The pasuk describes Torah as life and healing: כי חיים הם למצאיהם ולכל בשרו מרפא — Mishlei 4:22. The educational question is how a student encounters Torah as guidance within the life he is actually living.

A boy may understand the words of a source while remaining unsure how they relate to his own frustration, ambition, relationships, or decisions. Discussion gives those connections a place to be examined. What does the source say? What is the actual difficulty? How does the teaching change his understanding of the situation?

This is the purpose of connecting Torah study with self-awareness and practical reflection. A halacha, a passage of Mussar, or an idea in Chassidus can become relevant to a decision the boy is ready to consider. The educator helps preserve the meaning of the source while making space for that personal encounter.

### Teaching Torah as an Answer

A question gives learning direction. When a boy wants to understand a difficulty, relevant Torah sources become part of the search for an answer. The source is studied carefully, its reasoning is considered, and its implications are discussed.

That process does not depend on every boy asking the same question or reaching the same level at the same time. The educator works with the interests and understanding of the boys present. One question may open a connected subject, and the discussion can move through several sources while remaining grounded in the Torah itself.

Torah learning also carries obligations and requires sustained effort. Personal relevance gives the learner a way to participate in that effort with greater awareness. The aim is for the boy to understand more, identify with what he is learning, and increasingly direct his actions through it.

### The Educational Environment

This kind of learning requires an educator who listens, knows the sources, and lives the values being discussed. The relationship and atmosphere are part of the experience. Students need room to express a question honestly, consider an answer, and return to it as their understanding develops.

The morning Kodesh pods apply this through the [organic flow of Torah](#p02-learning-pods): questions, relevant sources, discussion, and individual guidance. The fuller [Academy 2027–28](#p03-academy-202728) vision connects that learning with practical work and responsibilities within the community.

Related reading: [Ratzon and Intrinsic Motivation](#a19-ratzon-and-intrinsic-motivation) · [Role Models, Or Pnimi, and Or Makif](#a22-role-models-or-pnimi-and-or-makif).

Torah references: [Tanya, chapter 48](https://www.chabad.org/library/tanya/tanya_cdo/aid/1196056/jewish/Tanya-Chapter-48-Part-1.htm); Mishlei 4:22. The educational application is BNA's synthesis of these ideas.

## HA01 מסגרת אלטרנטיבית לבנים בדרום פלורידה: מה ההורים באמת מחפשים

Route: `/he/blog/alternative-torah-learning-south-florida`  
Topic: סביבת הלימוד  
Search title: מסגרת לימוד תורה לבנים בדרום פלורידה | בני נביאים  
Search description: קבוצת לימודי קודש בבקרים בדרום פלורידה, עם מטרות אישיות, קשר עם מחנך ואחריות משותפת. כשעתיים עד שעתיים וחצי; מיקום ושעות בתיאום.

כאשר הורים מחפשים מסגרת אלטרנטיבית בדרום פלורידה, הם בדרך כלל לא מחפשים משהו נוצץ. הם מחפשים מקום שבו הבן שלהם יכול לנשום.

לפעמים הילד רשום לבית ספר או לישיבה, אבל בפועל הוא כבר לא שם. הוא יושב בחדר, אבל העיניים כבויות. הוא חכם, אבל לא מחובר. הוא רגיש, אבל מתנהג בקשיחות.

זה לא תמיד אומר שהילד מקולקל. פעמים רבות זה אומר שהסביבה לא מצליחה להגיע אליו.

בני נביאים היא סביבת לימוד תורה בדרום פלורידה לבנים שלא מוצאים את מקומם במסגרת הרגילה. קבוצת הלימוד הנוכחית נפגשת בבוקר, פנים אל פנים, למשך כשעתיים עד שעתיים וחצי, ומתמקדת בלימודי קודש בלבד, [מטרות אישיות](#ha05-אחריות-אישית-בחינוך-יהודי), חונכות, אחריות משותפת, תנועה לפי הצורך וקשר אמיתי לתורה. ההורים מביאים את הבנים ואוספים אותם בסיום. הרכב הגילים מותאם לבנים המשתתפים; המיקום בדרום פלורידה והשעות המדויקות ייקבעו בתיאום.

זו אינה מסגרת קלינית או טיפולית. זו סביבת לימוד תורה קטנה, רגועה ומבוססת קשר.

צרו קשר עם בני נביאים כדי לבדוק אם הסביבה הזאת מתאימה לבן שלכם.

הרבה הורים שמחפשים מסגרת לילדים עם ADHD בדרום פלורידה לא בהכרח מחפשים אבחון. הם מחפשים מקום שבו הבן שלהם לא מרגיש כמו בעיה בכל פעם שהגוף שלו צריך לזוז.

בני נביאים אינה תוכנית קלינית ואינה מאבחנת או מטפלת ב-ADHD. היא סביבת לימוד תורה קטנה, רגועה ומבוססת קשר, שיכולה להתאים לחלק מהבנים עם אתגרי קשב.

בקבוצת הלימוד יש לימודי קודש, [מטרות אישיות](#ha05-אחריות-אישית-בחינוך-יהודי) וחונכות. כאשר ילד מתקשה להמשיך, אפשר לבחון אם הפסקת תנועה קצרה עוזרת לו לחזור ללמידה.

אם הבן שלכם מתקשה במסגרת הרגילה וצריך סביבה קטנה ומבוססת קשר, דברו איתנו.

חינוך יהודי עצמי אינו אומר לעשות כלום. הוא אינו הפקר, ואינו אומר שהילד מנהל את החדר בלי להתחשב באחרים.

המשמעות היא התייחסות רצינית לעולם הפנימי של הילד. ילדים רבים התרגלו לזוז רק כאשר מישהו דוחף אותם בפרס, איום, ציון, עונש או אכזבה.

אחרי שנים כאלה ילד יכול לאבד קשר עם הרצון הפנימי שלו ללמוד. הוא עשוי להזדקק לזמן להפחתת הלחץ ולבניית היכולת ליזום, לקבל החלטות ולפעול בעצמו.

בסביבה תורנית, אוטונומיה מתקיימת בתוך מבנה ו[אחריות משותפת](#ha05-אחריות-אישית-בחינוך-יהודי). הילד נשאל מה הוא חושב, מה האפשרויות שלו, מה עשוי לקרות בעקבות החלטתו, והאם ההחלטה מתאימה לאדם שהוא רוצה להיות.

בני נביאים משתמשת במטרות אישיות, שיחות כנות, תנועה לפי הצורך ולימוד תורה משמעותי כדי לבנות אחריות פנימית.

אם הבן שלכם זקוק לאוטונומיה עם מבנה ואחריות משותפת, קבוצת לימוד של בני נביאים עשויה להתאים.

אחריות אישית אינה עצמאות בלי גבולות. היא היכולת של ילד להתחיל לנהל את עצמו מתוך תורה, מציאות ואחריות משותפת.

הרבה מסגרות מלמדות ילדים לחכות לשליטה חיצונית: לשבת כי אמרו, ללמוד כי יש מבחן, להתנהג כי יש עונש, ולהצליח כי יש פרס.

הכלים האלה יכולים ליצור סדר, אבל הם לא בהכרח יוצרים ילד שיודע לקבל החלטה אחראית כשאף אחד לא מסתכל.

בבני נביאים נקבעות עם כל בן התחייבויות לימודיות בהתאם לרמתו. הוא מברר עם המחנך מה דורשת השתתפות פעילה בלימוד, בודק אם עמד בהתחייבות שלו, ומשוחח בפרטיות על מה עזר ומה הפריע. ההתקדמות נבחנת ביחס אליו: מה הצליח לעשות, מה הקשה עליו ומה הצעד הבא.

המטרה היא שילד יחבר בין המעשים שלו לבין הערכים שלו: איזה יהודי אני רוצה להיות, מה ה׳ רוצה ממני עכשיו, ומה אני בוחר מחר.

למדו עוד על הדרך שבה בני נביאים בונה אחריות אישית דרך לימוד תורה, חונכות, מעקב ו[שותפות עם ההורים](#ha06-תפקיד-ההורים-בתוכנית-לימוד-תורה-אלטרנטיבית).

תוכנית לימוד תורה אלטרנטיבית אינה מקום שבו ההורים מוסרים את האחריות ומחכים שמישהו יתקן את הבן שלהם.

ההורים הם שותפים. זה לא אומר שהם צריכים לרחף מעל כל פרט או להפוך כל שיחה לדרשה. זה אומר שהשפה בבית צריכה לתמוך באותה מטרה: היכולת של הבן ליזום, לקבל החלטות ולפעול באחריות.

ילד שלומד [אחריות אישית](#ha05-אחריות-אישית-בחינוך-יהודי) צריך מבוגרים ששואלים שאלות טובות: למה התחייבת, מה קרה, מה למדת על עצמך, ומה הצעד הכנה הבא שלך.

אם הבית מדבר בעיקר בשפה של פרסים, איומים ומאבקי כוח, הילד עלול ללמוד להתמקח עם לחץ חיצוני. אם הבית מדבר בשפה של אחריות כנה, הילד יכול להתחיל לשים לב לעצמו ולבחור בבגרות.

בני נביאים פועלת טוב יותר כשהבית והמסגרת מדברים יחד בשפה של כבוד, אחריות משותפת, תנועה כשצריך ומעקב כנה. ההורים מסייעים לבן להגיע מוכן, משתפים בתצפיות מהבית, ומתאמים מטרות ופתרונות עם המחנך ועם הבן.

דברו עם בני נביאים על הדרך שבה שותפות הורים תומכת בצמיחה של הבן שלכם.

faq.question: What is available now?
faq.answer: In-person Kodesh learning pods for boys in South Florida, with parent drop-off. The current offer is Torah learning. The separate academy is planned for 2027–28.

faq.question: Are the pods online or in person?
faq.answer: In person.

faq.question: Do parents stay during the session?
faq.answer: Parents drop off their sons. The group's arrival, collection, and participation arrangements are confirmed before attendance.

faq.question: Which ages are grouped together?
faq.answer: Grouping depends on the boys who register, their learning levels, and their readiness. Mixed-age groups are possible. Include your son's age when you sign up so suitable arrangements can be discussed.

faq.question: What Torah subjects are taught?
faq.answer: Learning can draw on Chumash and Tanach, Mishnah and Gemara, Halacha, Mussar, and Chassidus. Relevant sources are identified as the group pursues questions and connected topics. The material and depth are suited to the boys present.

faq.question: Is there a fixed syllabus?
faq.answer: The group follows an organic flow of Torah learning. Sources are studied carefully as questions arise, and the educator connects related subjects. Specific reading and learning needs are also considered when arranging the group.

faq.question: Are secular studies or practical projects included in the learning pods?
faq.answer: The learning pods are dedicated to Kodesh. Practical projects and a full-day educational setting belong to the separate Academy 2027–28 model.

faq.question: Can a homeschool family join?
faq.answer: Yes. The Kodesh pods can form part of a family's wider educational arrangements. Parents remain responsible for their child's overall education and any applicable home-education requirements. Florida families can consult the [Florida Department of Education's home-education resources](https://www.fldoe.org/schools/school-choice/home-edu/parent-resources.stml).

faq.question: What does autonomy mean in practice?
faq.answer: Students take an active role in their learning and commitments. The educator provides clear boundaries, appropriate instruction, and follow-up suited to the student's level. Autonomy includes responsibility for how a choice affects the learning and other people.

faq.question: Can a boy step out of a lesson?
faq.answer: The model allows a boy to step out of an individual session within the agreed supervised setting. It does not give permission to leave the premises. Participation agreements and follow-up remain part of the learning.

faq.question: Are there minimum commitments?
faq.answer: Yes. Commitments are agreed according to the boy's level and the group arrangements. They provide a clear basis for participation and coaching.

faq.question: What happens when a commitment is not met?
faq.answer: The educator reviews what was agreed, what happened, and the difficulty encountered. The student is involved in deciding a practical next step, and the agreement is followed up. Parents are included when the difficulty requires collaboration between home and the learning group.

faq.question: What does individual coaching involve?
faq.answer: Private conversations about goals, progress, obstacles, and decisions. The emphasis is on helping the boy understand his own actions and take responsibility for the next step.

faq.question: How is progress assessed?
faq.answer: Progress is considered relative to the boy's current level. The review distinguishes an achieved task from the consistency, independence, and responsibility shown over time.

faq.question: How does the point system work?
faq.answer: Points reflect achievement of individually agreed goals and the difficulty of those goals. The criteria for a particular group or academy arrangement will be explained before they are used.

faq.question: How do you handle disagreement or conflict?
faq.answer: The students are helped to describe what happened, listen to the other perspective, consider the effect of their actions, and agree on a constructive response. Respectful disagreement, accountability, and relationship repair are practiced within the group.

faq.question: What happens if there is bullying or repeated intimidation?
faq.answer: The educator intervenes and addresses the behavior with the students and parents involved. Respect and safety are conditions of participation. Continued participation is reviewed when those conditions cannot be maintained.

faq.question: Can students ask difficult questions about Torah or Judaism?
faq.answer: Yes. Questions are taken seriously and examined through relevant sources and respectful discussion. The educator helps the group distinguish a question, an interpretation, and what a source actually says.

faq.question: Can a boy join if he needs support with Hebrew reading or attention?
faq.answer: Discuss his current abilities and the support he needs before enrollment. Group suitability and any additional instruction are considered individually. The learning pods offer Torah learning and educational coaching; specialized support should not be assumed from the program description.

faq.question: Does BNA provide therapy or clinical treatment?
faq.answer: The learning pods provide Torah education and coaching in participation, communication, and responsibility. A need for clinical treatment or specialist educational support should be discussed separately with the appropriate professional.

faq.question: What is expected of parents?
faq.answer: Parents support agreed expectations at home, help their sons arrive prepared, communicate relevant observations, and work with the educator when a difficulty arises. The [Parent Guide](#p17-parent-guide) explains this partnership.

faq.question: How are parents kept informed?
faq.answer: The educator and parent agree on the relevant communication arrangements. Updates focus on commitments, progress, difficulties, and the support that is useful to the student.

faq.question: What is the phone and internet policy?
faq.answer: Device arrangements are provided with the group's participation details. The educational approach to technology is explained in [A Guide to Healthy Technology Use](#a11-a-guide-to-healthy-technology-use-our-philosophy-and-approach).

faq.question: What should my son bring?
faq.answer: The required sefarim, materials, and other practical details are confirmed for the group before attendance.

faq.question: Are trips included?
faq.answer: Trips are part of the wider academy vision. Any specific trip has its own arrangements and information. A learning-pod inquiry does not reserve or pay for a trip.

faq.question: What does it cost?
faq.answer: Registering interest is free. Tuition and participation terms are provided before enrollment. No payment is collected through the initial interest form.

faq.question: Can funding or a scholarship be used?
faq.answer: Funding eligibility has not been confirmed for this offer. Confirm the actual provider, program, and funding requirements before relying on a scholarship or reimbursement.

faq.question: How is the academy different from the learning pods?
faq.answer: The academy is the planned academy model combining Torah learning, practical projects, individual coaching, and responsibilities within the institution.

faq.question: What are hard skills and soft skills?
faq.answer: Hard skills are specific capabilities, such as gardening, irrigation, measurement, or using a tool correctly. Soft skills concern how the work is carried out: consistency, independence, responsibility, communication, collaboration, and respectful disagreement.

faq.question: What decisions can students participate in?
faq.answer: The academy model includes student participation in budgeting, trip planning, organization, and other decisions within an agreed scope. Some decisions can be put to a student vote. Educators remain responsible for the boundaries of each activity and role.

faq.question: Will students have paid roles?
faq.answer: Paid roles are part of the longer-term contribution model for students who meet the requirements of a suitable role. They depend on demonstrated skills, responsibility, and the applicable employment requirements. No paid role is promised through interest registration.

faq.question: Will tuition decrease as a student takes more responsibility?
faq.answer: That is part of the intended academy model. The criteria and amounts still need to be set, and families will receive the actual tuition terms before enrollment.

faq.question: Can I express interest in both a pod and the academy?
faq.answer: Yes. The first question on the form lets you select a learning pod, Academy 2027–28, or both.

faq.question: What happens after I submit the form?
faq.answer: Shloimie follows up using the contact details you provide. The conversation addresses your son's age, current learning, location, and a suitable next step.

faq.question: Does the form enroll my son?
faq.answer: It records your interest and starts a conversation. Actual enrollment follows the discussion of the group, schedule, tuition, and participation terms.

faq.question: מה מוצע כעת?
faq.answer: קבוצות לימודי קודש, פנים אל פנים, לבנים בדרום פלורידה. ההורים מביאים את הבנים למסגרת ואינם נשארים למפגש. ההצעה הנוכחית היא לימוד תורה. האקדמיה הנפרדת מתוכננת לשנת הלימודים 2027–28.

faq.question: האם הלימוד מקוון או פנים אל פנים?
faq.answer: פנים אל פנים.

faq.question: האם ההורים נשארים במהלך המפגש?
faq.answer: ההורים מביאים את בניהם ואינם נשארים למפגש. סידורי ההגעה, האיסוף וההשתתפות של הקבוצה ייקבעו לפני תחילת ההשתתפות.

faq.question: אילו גילים לומדים יחד?
faq.answer: הרכב הקבוצה תלוי בבנים שנרשמים, ברמות הלימוד ובמידת המוכנות שלהם. ייתכנו קבוצות רב־גיליות. ציינו בהרשמה את גיל בנכם כדי שאפשר יהיה לדון בהרכב מתאים.

faq.question: אילו תחומי תורה נלמדים?
faq.answer: הלימוד יכול לכלול חומש ותנ״ך, משנה וגמרא, הלכה, מוסר וחסידות. מקורות רלוונטיים נבחרים כשהקבוצה מעמיקה בשאלות ובנושאים הקשורים אליהן. החומר ורמת העומק מותאמים לבנים הנוכחים.

faq.question: האם יש תוכנית לימודים קבועה?
faq.answer: הלימוד בקבוצה מתקדם בזרימה אורגנית של תורה. המקורות נלמדים בעיון מתוך השאלות שעולות, והמחנך מחבר בין נושאים קשורים. בעת הרכבת הקבוצה מובאים בחשבון גם צרכים מסוימים בקריאה ובלימוד.

faq.question: האם קבוצות הלימוד כוללות לימודי חול או פרויקטים מעשיים?
faq.answer: קבוצות הלימוד מוקדשות ללימודי קודש. פרויקטים מעשיים ומסגרת חינוכית ליום מלא שייכים למודל הנפרד של האקדמיה לשנת הלימודים 2027–28.

faq.question: האם משפחה בחינוך ביתי יכולה להצטרף?
faq.answer: כן. קבוצות לימודי הקודש יכולות להשתלב במסגרת החינוכית הרחבה של המשפחה. ההורים נשארים אחראים לחינוך הכולל של ילדם ולכל דרישה החלה על חינוך ביתי. משפחות בפלורידה יכולות לעיין ב[מידע להורים על חינוך ביתי של מחלקת החינוך של פלורידה](https://www.fldoe.org/schools/school-choice/home-edu/parent-resources.stml).

faq.question: מה פירושה של אוטונומיה בפועל?
faq.answer: התלמידים שותפים פעילים בלימוד ובהתחייבויות שלהם. המחנך מספק גבולות ברורים, הוראה מתאימה ומעקב המותאם לרמת התלמיד. אוטונומיה כוללת אחריות להשפעת ההחלטות על הלימוד ועל אנשים אחרים.

faq.question: האם בן יכול לצאת משיעור?
faq.answer: המודל מאפשר לבן לצאת ממפגש לימוד מסוים ולהישאר במסגרת המוסכמת שבה מתקיימת השגחה. אין בכך רשות לעזוב את המקום. ההסכמות בנוגע להשתתפות והמעקב אחריהן נשארים חלק מהלימוד.

faq.question: האם יש התחייבויות מינימום?
faq.answer: כן. ההתחייבויות נקבעות בהסכמה בהתאם לרמת הבן ולסידורי הקבוצה. הן מספקות בסיס ברור להשתתפות ולליווי.

faq.question: מה קורה כאשר התחייבות אינה מתקיימת?
faq.answer: המחנך בוחן מה סוכם, מה קרה ומה היה הקושי. התלמיד שותף להחלטה על הצעד המעשי הבא, ובהמשך בודקים כיצד ההסכמה מיושמת. ההורים מצטרפים לתהליך כאשר הקושי מצריך שיתוף פעולה בין הבית לקבוצת הלימוד.

faq.question: מה כולל ליווי אישי?
faq.answer: שיחות פרטיות על מטרות, התקדמות, מכשולים והחלטות. הדגש הוא על סיוע לבן להבין את מעשיו ולקבל אחריות לצעד הבא.

faq.question: כיצד מעריכים את ההתקדמות?
faq.answer: ההתקדמות נבחנת ביחס לרמתו הנוכחית של הבן. ההערכה מבחינה בין משימה שהושלמה לבין העקביות, העצמאות והאחריות שניכרות לאורך זמן.

faq.question: כיצד פועלת שיטת הניקוד?
faq.answer: הנקודות משקפות עמידה במטרות אישיות שסוכמו ואת מידת הקושי שלהן. הקריטריונים של קבוצה או מסגרת באקדמיה יוסברו לפני תחילת השימוש בהם.

faq.question: כיצד מתמודדים עם מחלוקת או סכסוך?
faq.answer: מסייעים לתלמידים לתאר מה קרה, להקשיב לנקודת המבט האחרת, לבחון את השפעת מעשיהם ולהסכים על תגובה בונה. מחלוקת מכבדת, קבלת אחריות ותיקון הקשר מתורגלים בתוך הקבוצה.

faq.question: מה קורה במקרה של בריונות או הפחדה חוזרת?
faq.answer: המחנך מתערב ומטפל בהתנהגות עם התלמידים וההורים המעורבים. כבוד ובטיחות הם תנאים להשתתפות. כאשר אי אפשר לשמור על תנאים אלה, המשך ההשתתפות נבחן מחדש.

faq.question: האם התלמידים יכולים לשאול שאלות קשות על התורה או על היהדות?
faq.answer: כן. השאלות נלקחות ברצינות ונבחנות באמצעות מקורות רלוונטיים ודיון מכבד. המחנך מסייע לקבוצה להבחין בין שאלה, פרשנות ומה שהמקור אומר בפועל.

faq.question: האם בן שזקוק לתמיכה בקריאה בעברית או בקשב יכול להצטרף?
faq.answer: לפני ההרשמה יש לשוחח על יכולותיו הנוכחיות ועל התמיכה שהוא צריך. ההתאמה לקבוצה והצורך בהוראה נוספת נבחנים באופן אישי. קבוצות הלימוד מציעות לימוד תורה וליווי חינוכי; אין להניח שתיאור התוכנית כולל תמיכה מקצועית ייעודית.

faq.question: האם BNA מציעה טיפול נפשי או טיפול קליני?
faq.answer: קבוצות הלימוד מציעות חינוך תורני וליווי בהשתתפות, בתקשורת ובאחריות. צורך בטיפול קליני או בתמיכה חינוכית מקצועית ייעודית יש לבחון בנפרד עם איש המקצוע המתאים.

faq.question: מה מצופה מההורים?
faq.answer: ההורים מחזקים בבית את הציפיות שסוכמו, עוזרים לבניהם להגיע מוכנים, משתפים בתצפיות רלוונטיות ועובדים עם המחנך כאשר מתעורר קושי. [מדריך ההורים](#hp17-מדריך-ההורים) מסביר את השותפות הזאת.

faq.question: כיצד ההורים מתעדכנים?
faq.answer: המחנך וההורה מסכמים את אופן התקשורת המתאים. העדכונים מתמקדים בהתחייבויות, בהתקדמות, בקשיים ובתמיכה המועילה לתלמיד.

faq.question: מהי המדיניות בנוגע לטלפונים ולאינטרנט?
faq.answer: ההנחיות בנוגע למכשירים יימסרו עם פרטי ההשתתפות של הקבוצה. הגישה החינוכית לטכנולוגיה מוסברת ב[מדריך לשימוש בריא בטכנולוגיה](#ha04-שימוש-בריא-בטכנולוגיה-לילדים-יהודים).

faq.question: מה על בני להביא?
faq.answer: הספרים הנדרשים, החומרים ושאר הפרטים המעשיים ייקבעו עבור הקבוצה לפני תחילת ההשתתפות.

faq.question: האם טיולים כלולים?
faq.answer: טיולים הם חלק מהחזון הרחב של האקדמיה. לכל טיול מסוים יהיו סידורים ומידע משלו. פנייה בנוגע לקבוצת לימוד אינה שומרת מקום בטיול ואינה משלמת עליו.

faq.question: מהי העלות?
faq.answer: הרשמה להתעניינות היא ללא תשלום. שכר הלימוד ותנאי ההשתתפות יימסרו לפני ההרשמה בפועל. לא נגבה תשלום בטופס ההתעניינות הראשוני.

faq.question: האם אפשר להשתמש במימון או במלגה?
faq.answer: טרם אושרה זכאות למימון עבור ההצעה הזאת. לפני שמסתמכים על מלגה או החזר, יש לבדוק את נותן השירות בפועל, את התוכנית ואת דרישות המימון.

faq.question: במה שונה האקדמיה מקבוצות הלימוד?
faq.answer: האקדמיה היא המודל המתוכנן לאקדמיה, המשלב לימוד תורה, פרויקטים מעשיים, ליווי אישי ותפקידים במסגרת.

faq.question: מהן מיומנויות טכניות ומיומנויות רכות?
faq.answer: מיומנויות טכניות הן יכולות מוגדרות, כגון גינון, השקיה, מדידה או שימוש נכון בכלי עבודה. מיומנויות רכות נוגעות לאופן ביצוע העבודה: עקביות, עצמאות, אחריות, תקשורת, שיתוף פעולה ומחלוקת מכבדת.

faq.question: באילו החלטות התלמידים יכולים להשתתף?
faq.answer: מודל האקדמיה כולל השתתפות תלמידים בתקצוב, בתכנון טיולים, בארגון ובהחלטות נוספות בתחום מוסכם. אפשר להעמיד חלק מההחלטות להצבעת התלמידים. המחנכים נשארים אחראים לגבולות של כל פעילות ותפקיד.

faq.question: האם יהיו לתלמידים תפקידים בתשלום?
faq.answer: תפקידים בתשלום הם חלק ממודל התרומה לטווח הארוך, עבור תלמידים שעומדים בדרישות של תפקיד מתאים. הם תלויים במיומנויות שהוכחו, באחריות ובדרישות התעסוקה החלות על התפקיד. הרשמה להתעניינות אינה מבטיחה תפקיד בתשלום.

faq.question: האם שכר הלימוד יפחת ככל שהתלמיד יקבל יותר אחריות?
faq.answer: זהו חלק מהמודל המיועד לאקדמיה. הקריטריונים והסכומים עדיין צריכים להיקבע, והמשפחות יקבלו את תנאי שכר הלימוד בפועל לפני ההרשמה.

faq.question: האם אפשר להביע עניין גם בקבוצת לימוד וגם באקדמיה?
faq.answer: כן. בשאלה הראשונה בטופס אפשר לבחור קבוצת לימוד, את האקדמיה לשנת הלימודים 2027–28, או את שתיהן.

faq.question: מה קורה לאחר שליחת הטופס?
faq.answer: שלומי ייצור קשר באמצעות הפרטים שמסרתם. השיחה תעסוק בגיל בנכם, בלימוד הנוכחי שלו, במיקום ובצעד הבא המתאים.

faq.question: האם הטופס רושם את בני לתוכנית?
faq.answer: הטופס מתעד את ההתעניינות שלכם ופותח שיחה. ההרשמה בפועל נעשית לאחר הדיון בקבוצה, בלוח הזמנים, בשכר הלימוד ובתנאי ההשתתפות.

## P04 Teaching Philosophy

Route: `/teaching-philosophy`  
Search title: Teaching Philosophy | Torah, Agency, and Responsibility | BNA  
Search description: The BNA educational philosophy: ratzon, intrinsic motivation, authentic relationships, role models, self-governance, and meaningful responsibility.

### Torah Knowledge Expressed in Life

Education develops the understanding, abilities, and character a person needs to fulfill his purpose. At BNA, Torah gives that purpose direction. Learning becomes personal through the questions a boy pursues, the example of the people around him, and the responsibilities he accepts.

The practical model rests on autonomy, agency, and shared responsibility. The articles below explain the thinking behind it.

### Ratzon and Intrinsic Motivation

Ratzon is the learner's inner will: what he wants to understand, become, and accomplish. [Intrinsic motivation](#a19-ratzon-and-intrinsic-motivation) concerns interest in the learning itself. Meaningful commitments also develop as a boy identifies with the values and responsibilities he chooses to take on.

Article: [Ratzon and Intrinsic Motivation](#a19-ratzon-and-intrinsic-motivation)  
Related article: [Torah Learning Without Bribes, Yelling, or Fake Motivation](#a05-torah-learning-without-bribes-yelling-or-fake-motivation)

### Responsibility Through Participation

Responsibility requires a real role, a meaningful task, and an opportunity to follow through. A boy learns from the effect of his work, including mistakes, while receiving guidance that helps him understand and improve his decisions.

Article: [Responsibility Through Meaningful Contribution](#a20-responsibility-through-meaningful-contribution)

### Self-Governance

Self-governance connects values with action. It includes recognizing a situation, considering possible responses, making a commitment, and reviewing what actually happened. The educator helps the student develop this process rather than taking over every decision.

Article: [Self-Governance in Jewish Education](#a09-self-governance-in-jewish-education)

### The Learning Environment

The physical space, the available resources, the people, and the atmosphere around learning all shape the experience. An environment should make meaningful activity possible and give boys a reason to participate.

Article: [Designing the Learning Environment](#a21-designing-the-learning-environment)

### Educators and Role Models

Instruction helps a boy understand something at his present level. A role model gives him a picture of what he can become. BNA's educational use of [Or Pnimi and Or Makif](#a22-role-models-or-pnimi-and-or-makif) distinguishes these complementary influences.

Article: [Role Models, Or Pnimi, and Or Makif](#a22-role-models-or-pnimi-and-or-makif)  
Related article: [Does Your Son Connect to His Rebbe?](#a13-does-your-son-connect-to-his-rebbe)

### Torah and Inner Development

Torah learning includes study, reflection, and the integration of understanding into life. Chassidus gives language to the relationship between what is already understood and what inspires a person beyond his present understanding.

Article: [Torah, Daas, and Inner Development](#a23-torah-daas-and-inner-development)

### The Organic Flow of Torah

The practical learning begins with the group: its questions, interests, and present understanding. Relevant sources are studied as the discussion moves between connected subjects.

Article: [Torah That Answers Real Life](#a10-torah-that-answers-real-life)  
Program page: [Morning Kodesh Learning](#p02-learning-pods)

### Parents as Partners

Parents contribute knowledge of their child, reinforce agreed expectations, and work with the educator when difficulties arise. Consistent collaboration gives the boy support while preserving his responsibility for his own choices.

Article: [The Parent's Role](#a08-the-parents-role-in-an-alternative-torah-learning-program)  
Practical guide: [Parent Guide](#p17-parent-guide)

Text link: [All Articles](#p05-article-library)

## HP04 הגישה החינוכית

Route: `/he/teaching-philosophy`  
Search title: הגישה החינוכית | תורה, יוזמה ואחריות | BNA  
Search description: הגישה החינוכית של BNA: רצון, מוטיבציה פנימית, קשרים אותנטיים, דמויות מופת, ניהול עצמי ואחריות משמעותית.

### הבנת התורה וביטויה בחיים

החינוך מפתח את ההבנה, היכולות והמידות שאדם זקוק להן כדי למלא את ייעודו. ב־BNA התורה נותנת לייעוד הזה כיוון. הלימוד נעשה אישי דרך השאלות שהבן מבקש לברר, הדוגמה של האנשים סביבו והאחריות שהוא מקבל על עצמו.

המודל המעשי נשען על אוטונומיה, היכולת ליזום ולפעול ואחריות משותפת. המאמרים הבאים מסבירים את החשיבה שמאחוריו.

### רצון ומוטיבציה פנימית

הרצון הוא שאיפתו הפנימית של הלומד: מה הוא רוצה להבין, להיות ולהשיג. [מוטיבציה פנימית (מאמר באנגלית)](#a19-ratzon-and-intrinsic-motivation) נוגעת לעניין בלימוד עצמו. גם התחייבויות משמעותיות מתפתחות כאשר הבן מזדהה עם הערכים ועם האחריות שהוא בוחר לקבל על עצמו.

מאמר: [רצון ומוטיבציה פנימית (מאמר באנגלית)](#a19-ratzon-and-intrinsic-motivation)  
מאמר קשור: [לימוד תורה בלי שוחד, צעקות או מוטיבציה מלאכותית (מאמר באנגלית)](#a05-torah-learning-without-bribes-yelling-or-fake-motivation)

### אחריות מתוך השתתפות

אחריות דורשת תפקיד ממשי, משימה משמעותית והזדמנות להשלים התחייבות. הבן לומד מהשפעת עבודתו, גם מטעויות, ומקבל הדרכה המסייעת לו להבין את החלטותיו ולשפר אותן.

מאמר: [אחריות באמצעות תרומה משמעותית (מאמר באנגלית)](#a20-responsibility-through-meaningful-contribution)

### ניהול עצמי

ניהול עצמי מחבר בין ערכים לפעולה. הוא כולל הכרה במצב, בחינת תגובות אפשריות, קבלת התחייבות ובדיקה של מה שקרה בפועל. המחנך מסייע לתלמיד לפתח את התהליך הזה ולהיות שותף פעיל בהחלטותיו.

מאמר: [אחריות אישית בחינוך יהודי](#ha05-אחריות-אישית-בחינוך-יהודי)

### סביבת הלימוד

המרחב הפיזי, המשאבים הזמינים, האנשים והאווירה סביב הלימוד מעצבים יחד את החוויה. הסביבה צריכה לאפשר עשייה משמעותית ולתת לבנים סיבה להשתתף.

מאמר: [עיצוב סביבת הלימוד (מאמר באנגלית)](#a21-designing-the-learning-environment)

### מחנכים ודמויות מופת

הוראה מסייעת לבן להבין דבר בהתאם לרמתו הנוכחית. דמות מופת ממחישה לו מה הוא יכול להיות. השימוש החינוכי של BNA במושגים [אור פנימי ואור מקיף (מאמר באנגלית)](#a22-role-models-or-pnimi-and-or-makif) מבחין בין שתי ההשפעות המשלימות האלה.

מאמר: [דמויות מופת, אור פנימי ואור מקיף (מאמר באנגלית)](#a22-role-models-or-pnimi-and-or-makif)  
מאמר קשור: [האם בנכם קשור לרבי שלו? (מאמר באנגלית)](#a13-does-your-son-connect-to-his-rebbe)

### תורה והתפתחות פנימית

לימוד התורה כולל עיון, התבוננות ושילוב ההבנה בחיים. החסידות נותנת שפה לקשר שבין מה שאדם כבר מבין לבין מה שמעורר בו השראה מעבר להבנתו הנוכחית.

מאמר: [תורה, דעת והתפתחות פנימית (מאמר באנגלית)](#a23-torah-daas-and-inner-development)

### זרימה אורגנית של לימוד התורה

הלימוד בפועל מתחיל בקבוצה: בשאלותיה, בתחומי העניין שלה ובהבנתה הנוכחית. לומדים מקורות מתאימים ככל שהדיון מתקדם בין נושאים קשורים.

מאמר: [תורה הנותנת מענה לחיים עצמם (מאמר באנגלית)](#a10-torah-that-answers-real-life)  
עמוד התוכנית: [לימודי קודש בבוקר](#hp02-קבוצות-לימוד)

### ההורים כשותפים

ההורים מביאים את היכרותם עם ילדם, מחזקים ציפיות שסוכמו ועובדים עם המחנך כשעולים קשיים. שיתוף פעולה עקבי נותן לבן תמיכה ושומר על אחריותו להחלטותיו.

מאמר: [תפקיד ההורים](#ha06-תפקיד-ההורים-בתוכנית-לימוד-תורה-אלטרנטיבית)  
מדריך מעשי: [מדריך להורים](#hp17-מדריך-ההורים)

קישור: [כל המאמרים](#hp05-ספריית-המאמרים)

## P17 Parent Guide

Route: `/parents/guide`  
Search title: Parent Guide | Collaboration and Coaching | BNA  
Search description: How parents support preparation, goals, respectful communication, and follow-through in BNA's learning community.

### Parent Collaboration

The parent, student, and educator bring different knowledge to the same conversation. Parents know the child's history and daily life. The educator sees his participation in the learning environment. The boy needs to be involved in understanding the difficulty and taking responsibility for his response.

### Support the Shared Expectations

Help your son understand the commitments agreed with the group. Discuss what responsibility, respect, and appropriate disagreement look like in actual situations. Encourage him to describe his own part rather than speaking for him whenever a difficulty arises.

### Help Him Arrive Prepared

Support timely arrival, the necessary materials, and the practical arrangements for the morning. As his independence develops, transfer appropriate parts of that preparation to him and review whether they are being carried out reliably.

### Share Useful Observations

Tell the educator what you are seeing at home: changes in interest, difficulty preparing, a concern about a relationship, or a commitment that has become hard to maintain. Specific observations make it easier to agree on useful support.

### Work Through Difficulties Together

Clarify the situation before deciding what should happen next. Give your son time to explain his view. Consider the available responses, their likely effects, and which response fits the values and commitments involved.

An agreed next step should be specific enough to follow up. Review what happened and adjust the support where necessary.

### Allow Learning from Mistakes

A mistake can reveal a skill that needs practice, a task that was not understood, or a commitment that was unrealistic. The aim is to help the boy evaluate the result and take the next responsible action.

Adults keep appropriate boundaries while allowing room for the student to experience the consequences of manageable decisions. Coaching develops his judgment over time.

### Use the Appropriate Conversation

Individual learning, behavior, and family concerns are discussed privately with the educator. Community conversations concern shared arrangements and interests. Another child's private information does not belong in a parent group or directory.

### Review Progress

Notice both achievements and the conditions under which they occurred. A task completed with help, a task completed independently, and a responsibility maintained consistently are different forms of progress.

The parent–educator conversation should make those distinctions clear and identify a practical next step.

## HP17 מדריך ההורים

Route: `/he/parents/guide`  
Search title: מדריך ההורים | שיתוף פעולה וליווי | BNA  
Search description: כיצד ההורים תומכים בהכנה ללימוד, במטרות, בתקשורת מכבדת ובעמידה בהתחייבויות בקהילת הלימוד של BNA.

### שיתוף פעולה עם ההורים

ההורה, התלמיד והמחנך מביאים ידע שונה לאותה שיחה. ההורים מכירים את ההיסטוריה ואת חיי היומיום של הילד. המחנך רואה את השתתפותו בסביבת הלימוד. הבן צריך להיות שותף להבנת הקושי ולקבלת אחריות על תגובתו.

### חיזוק הציפיות המשותפות

עזרו לבנכם להבין את ההתחייבויות שסוכמו עם הקבוצה. שוחחו על האופן שבו אחריות, כבוד ומחלוקת ראויה מתבטאים במצבים ממשיים. עודדו אותו לתאר את חלקו שלו, במקום לדבר בשמו בכל פעם שעולה קושי.

### עזרו לו להגיע מוכן

סייעו בהגעה בזמן, בהבאת החומרים הדרושים ובסידורים המעשיים של הבוקר. ככל שעצמאותו מתפתחת, העבירו אליו חלקים מתאימים מההכנה ובדקו אם הוא מבצע אותם בעקביות.

### שיתוף בתצפיות מועילות

ספרו למחנך מה אתם רואים בבית: שינויים בעניין, קושי להתארגן, דאגה בנוגע לקשר עם אדם אחר או התחייבות שקשה לשמור עליה. תצפיות ממוקדות מקלות על ההסכמה על תמיכה מועילה.

### התמודדות משותפת עם קשיים

בררו את המצב לפני שמחליטים מה צריך לקרות בהמשך. תנו לבנכם זמן להסביר את נקודת מבטו. בחנו את התגובות האפשריות, את השפעתן הצפויה ואת ההתאמה שלהן לערכים ולהתחייבויות הנוגעים למצב.

הצעד הבא שסוכם צריך להיות ברור דיו כדי שאפשר יהיה לעקוב אחריו. בדקו מה קרה והתאימו את התמיכה לפי הצורך.

### למידה מטעויות

טעות יכולה להצביע על מיומנות שזקוקה לתרגול, על משימה שלא הובנה או על התחייבות שלא הייתה מציאותית. המטרה היא לעזור לבן להעריך את התוצאה ולנקוט את הצעד האחראי הבא.

המבוגרים שומרים על גבולות מתאימים, ובה בעת מאפשרים לתלמיד לחוות את תוצאותיהן של החלטות שהוא מסוגל להתמודד איתן. הליווי מפתח את שיקול דעתו לאורך זמן.

### בחירת מסגרת השיחה המתאימה

עניינים אישיים הנוגעים ללימוד, להתנהגות ולמשפחה נידונים בפרטיות עם המחנך. שיחות קהילתיות עוסקות בסידורים ובתחומי עניין משותפים. מידע פרטי על ילד אחר אינו שייך לקבוצת הורים או לאינדקס.

### בחינת ההתקדמות

שימו לב גם להישגים וגם לתנאים שבהם הושגו. משימה שהושלמה בעזרה, משימה שהושלמה באופן עצמאי ואחריות שנשמרה בעקביות הן צורות שונות של התקדמות.

השיחה בין ההורה למחנך צריכה להבהיר את ההבחנות האלה ולזהות צעד מעשי להמשך.
